Most experts note that both President Trump and President Putin have issued unusually strong public statements in favor of extending New START for one year, creating genuine diplomatic momentum. Base rates from previous arms control extensions (such as the 2021 New START extension) suggest last-minute deals—sometimes within days of deadline—are not rare when mutual interest and strong leader-level signaling are present. However, nearly all experts caution that significant procedural, technical, and political obstacles remain. These include the formalization requirement (a signed agreement, not just intent), suspended inspections and broader verification hurdles, severe time pressure (less than four months), ongoing conflicts (especially Ukraine), and potential bureaucratic or domestic opposition in both countries. While verification lapses raise doubts, the question only requires a signed agreement, not ratification or implemented reductions. The possibility for YES is considered meaningfully above the historical base rate for new arms control treaties, primarily due to clear top-level signaling and the low bar for resolution. However, failure remains likely if inertia, political headwinds, or late-stage setbacks prevent formal signature. All experts judge the trilateral or China-involved path as almost impossible before 2026. Probability estimates range widely based on discipline and weight on procedural hurdles: the low is 18%, and the high is 85%, but most cluster between 38% and 78%. The median expert assessment is that a last-minute US–Russia treaty extension is somewhat more likely than not, but well short of certainty, with most probabilities falling in the 60–72% range.
